explanations.answer: He starts crying out to Jesus
explanations.explanation: That's what he does, baker. When he hears it's Jesus of Nazareth, he begins to cry out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47). He can't see Jesus, so he uses the one thing he's got, his voice. And he uses ALL of it.

explanations.answer: He sends someone to bring Jesus
explanations.explanation: Nope, no messenger here, friend. Bartimaeus doesn't send anybody. He calls out himself, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47). I think he figured a message might not get there in time, but that's just my guess.

explanations.answer: He waits for the crowd to pass
explanations.explanation: Waiting would've been the quiet move, friend. But the text says that when he heard it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out (Mark 10:47). No waiting and no hoping the crowd would slow down. He speaks up while Jesus is right there.
Yep, silent. The text says many people admonished him to be silent (Mark 10:48). Admonished is a polite word for "hey, hush it." That's a lot of people telling one man to zip it.

Patient sounds nice and gentle, baker, but that's not the word. The text says many people admonished him to be silent (Mark 10:48). They weren't asking for patience, they wanted the noise to stop. Silent was the word.
Grateful is a good word, friend, but nobody says it here. The text says many people admonished him to be silent (Mark 10:48). It was a hush, not a thank-you note. Silent is the one.
That's the opposite of what happens, baker. The text says he cried out all the louder (Mark 10:48). Many people told him to be silent, and he got LOUDER. He didn't quiet down or wait for anything.

False is right. Many people admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder (Mark 10:48). He doesn't hush and he doesn't wait. I've had a few people tell me to quiet down in my day, and I did NOT handle it this well.

explanations.answer: He stops and has him called over
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” (Mark 10:49). A big crowd is moving, and one voice at the side of the road gets Jesus to stop. He hears Bartimaeus, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: He keeps walking and waves to him
explanations.explanation: No walking on by, friend. The text says Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” (Mark 10:49). A wave would've been over in a second, but Jesus stops the whole walk for this man.

explanations.answer: He sends a disciple to bless him
explanations.explanation: Close to the idea of sending somebody, but that's not what happens, baker. Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” (Mark 10:49). He has the man called over to Him. No blessing is passed along from a distance.

That's it, baker. They called the blind man and said, “Take courage!” and “Get up! He is calling for you.” (Mark 10:49). Think about that. A minute ago people were telling him to hush, and now they're cheering him on. Jesus calling changes the whole mood on that road.
Staying put is the old plan, friend, and the crowd drops it fast. They tell him, “Take courage!” and “Get up! He is calling for you.” (Mark 10:49). Nobody says wait. Jesus is calling him over.

explanations.answer: Ask quickly and keep it short
explanations.explanation: Nobody gives him a speech coach, baker. What they say is, “Take courage!” and “Get up! He is calling for you.” (Mark 10:49). There's no word about keeping it short. They just tell him to get up and come.

True. The text says, “Throwing off his cloak, Bartimaeus jumped up and came to Jesus.” (Mark 10:50). He doesn't shuffle or take his time. He JUMPS. I wish I moved like that when my oven timer goes off.
Flip that one, baker. The text says he jumped up and came to Jesus (Mark 10:50). He was told Jesus was calling, and up he went. No dragging his feet and no second thoughts.
Yep, see. He says, “Rabboni, let me see again.” (Mark 10:51). Rabboni is a respectful way to address a teacher. Jesus asked what he wanted, and Bartimaeus tells Him plainly.
Walking isn't what he asks for, friend. He says, “Rabboni, let me see again.” (Mark 10:51). He asks about his eyes. And he'd already shown he could get up and come to Jesus just fine.
Work is a fair guess for a man who was a beggar, baker, but that's not his request. He says, “Rabboni, let me see again.” (Mark 10:51). Jesus asks what he wants, and the answer is sight.
Not quite, baker. The text says, “And immediately he received his sight” (Mark 10:52). Jesus says a few words, and the sight comes right then. No waiting in line and no waiting on the clock.
False is right. Mark 10:52 says, “And immediately he received his sight…” There's no waiting period. Jesus speaks, and Bartimaeus can see.

explanations.answer: He follows Jesus along the road
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says he “followed Jesus along the road.” (Mark 10:52). Jesus told him, “Go,” and he could see, so he went the same way Jesus was going. I think that says a lot, but I'll let you chew on it.
Jericho is behind them, friend. The text says Jesus and His disciples were leaving it (Mark 10:46). Bartimaeus doesn't turn around. He followed Jesus along the road (Mark 10:52).

explanations.answer: He runs to tell his family
explanations.explanation: A fine idea if I'd written it, baker, but the text doesn't go there. It says he “followed Jesus along the road.” (Mark 10:52). His family isn't mentioned in the story at all. We only hear that he follows Jesus.
